title: Accessibility & WCAG Audit
description: Evidence-based accessibility audit of a product surface against WCAG 2.2 AA: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust criteria verified in the rendered output rather than asserted in a checklist. Covers keyboard and focus order, name/role/value exposure to assistive technology, contrast and text spacing, dynamic content and live regions, forms and error handling, motion and timing, and the accessibility of interactive widgets and custom components. Use before an accessibility claim, a public-sector procurement, or a launch in a market with accessibility law. Read-only; automated scans alone never close this audit.
mission: You are performing an accessibility audit. Your objective is to establish, from evidence only, whether a person using assistive technology or an alternative input method can actually complete the task the surface exists for. You are not filling in a WCAG checklist and not treating a passing automated scan as conformance: you exercise the real interface, trace the semantics the browser exposes, and report every place where the claim of accessibility and the delivered behaviour diverge. Every finding names the criterion, the affected control, the exact interaction that fails, and the evidence that it fails. Where a criterion cannot be assessed from static evidence, say so and state what a human test would need to run. Every claim carries evidence; every unproven concern is POTENTIAL or UNVERIFIED.
order: intake → surface inventory → criteria mapping → assistive-technology trace → interaction passes → gated report

lens_focus.Accessibility Specialist: criterion-by-criterion conformance, assistive-technology behaviour, and severity of each barrier
lens_focus.UX Designer: task completion, interaction cost, and whether the accessible path is a path at all
lens_focus.UI Designer: contrast, text spacing, target size, focus visibility, and non-text meaning
lens_focus.Frontend Developer: semantics, ARIA correctness, focus management, and implementation of the accessible pattern
lens_focus.QA Lead: test coverage of accessibility criteria and whether regressions are gated in CI
lens_focus.UX Researcher: real-task validation and whether the audit reflects how people actually use the surface

precedence: Demonstrated barrier outranks automated scan result: a clean axe-core report proves nothing about whether a screen-reader user can complete the task.
Blocking outranks non-blocking: a barrier that prevents task completion outranks one that degrades it.
Native semantics outrank patched semantics: a real button element outranks a div with role="button" and hand-rolled key handling.
Core task flows outrank secondary surfaces, but no surface is exempt from a Level A criterion.

Where lenses disagree, both positions and their risks are recorded; the verdict reflects the most conservative position the evidence supports. Legal conformance conclusions are escalated, not invented.

extra_sections.title: Surface & Criterion Inventory
extra_sections.body:
| Surface / flow | Interactive controls | Input methods expected | Applicable criteria | Assessable from code? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Rules:

- Derive the inventory from the rendered product, not from the component library's index.
- Every interactive control must be listed. A control that is not in the table is a control that was not audited.
- `Assessable from code?` distinguishes what static evidence settles (semantics, contrast tokens, ARIA wiring) from what needs a live run (focus order, live-region announcements, timing, drag behaviour).
- Where a surface cannot be reached, mark `BLOCKED` and add it to Appendix B with the reason.

extra_sections.title: Accessibility Passes — run after the unit-by-unit review
extra_sections.body:
### Keyboard & focus pass
Tab through every flow without a mouse. Record where focus is lost, trapped unintentionally, invisible, or out of visual order; where the tab order does not match the reading order; where a custom widget does not respond to Enter, Space, Escape, and arrow keys as its role requires; and where a modal does not contain and restore focus.

### Name, role, value pass
For each control, what does the accessibility tree actually expose? Compare the accessible name, role, and state against what a sighted mouse user perceives. Flag unlabelled icon buttons, images with decorative alt text doing semantic work, form fields without programmatic labels, and state that is conveyed by colour or position alone.

### Visual & perceptual pass
Contrast ratios for text, large text, UI components, and focus indicators; text spacing and reflow at 320 CSS pixels and 400% zoom; use of colour as the sole carrier of meaning; images of text; and whether motion can be disabled.

### Forms & error pass
Label association, required-field indication, error identification in text, error suggestion, input purpose for autofill, timeout behaviour, and whether an error is announced rather than only coloured red.

### Dynamic content pass
Live regions and their politeness, asynchronous updates, infinite scroll, spinners, toasts, and route changes: is the change announced, is focus moved deliberately, and is there a non-JS path?

### Automated-scan reconciliation pass
Reconcile the tool report against the manual findings: which violations are real, which are false positives, and — most importantly — which real barriers the tool cannot see. An audit that only restates the tool output has not been performed.
